title: Assessment of Nutritional Status of Infants Living in Arsenic-Contaminated Areas in Bangladesh and Its Association with Arsenic Exposure.
ehr_evidence: Trained field workers took anthropometric measurements such as weight and length of all participating infants at 3, 6 and 9 months of age, and interviewers collected information by face to face interview using a structured questionnaire; arsenic exposure was characterized from tube well drinking water samples analyzed by flow injection-hydride generation atomic absorption spectrometry.
summary: A prospective longitudinal cohort of 120 mother-infant pairs followed from birth to 9 months in an arsenic-contaminated rural area of Bangladesh assessed the association between household tube-well arsenic exposure (<50 vs ≥50 μg/L) and infant malnutrition (WAZ, HAZ, WHZ Z-scores).
key_findings: Stunting prevalence was 10% at 3 months and 44% at both 6 and 9 months of age.
Wasting was 23.3% at 3 months with no wasted infants at 6 and 9 months; underweight was 25% at 3 months and 10% at 6 months.
A significant association of stunting with household drinking water arsenic exposure ≥50 μg/L was observed only at 9 months of age (p = 0.009).
No significant association was found between household arsenic exposure and underweight or wasting (acute malnutrition) during infancy.
The significant stunting association at 9 months was interpreted as a likely statistical incongruity/anomaly given the small sample size and short follow-up.
captured_features: Infant weight and length/height measurements at 3, 6 and 9 months
Tube-well drinking water arsenic concentration (<50 vs ≥50 μg/L)
population: 120 mother-infant pairs (infants followed from birth to 9 months) in an arsenic-contaminated rural upazilla of Bangladesh
limitations: Small sample size (120 mother-infant pairs) limiting statistical power.
Exposure misclassification due to households changing drinking water sources after baseline water sampling.
No data captured on maternal or infant dietary/nutritional intake.
